name: Baskeet
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Treis, Yvonne & Alexander Werth. 2014. Notes from the Field: Baskeet Phonological Sketch and Digital Wordlist. Language Documentation & Conservation 8: 810-832. hdl:10125/24627 (open access, CC BY-NC).
catalog_locator: §2.3.1 Tonemes and §2.3.3 Tonological patterns, p. 818; caveat on earlier sources p. 811; question intonation fn 44-45, p. 828 (fn 46, p. 829).
catalog_quote: 2.3.1 TONEMES. Baskeet is a tonal language with two tonemes, high (H) and low (L). The syllable is the tone-bearing unit and tone occurs on each syllable. The importance of tone has so far been overlooked in the literature on Baskeet. Tone is, however, used to differentiate lexemes, and tonal minimal pairs are easily found, e.g. /zàrzàrá/ ‘lizard’ (Rec2-27) vs. /zàrzárà/ ‘sieve’ (Rec2-28) ... We can exclude that Baskeet is a, ‘pitch-accent language’ with (only) one high tone per word, as claimed by Sottile (2002: 34f) and Inui (2005: 3f). ... 2.3.3 TONOLOGICAL PATTERNS. All-low sequences do not occur on words in isolation. Therefore, each monosyllabic noun carries a high tone. For disyllabic nouns the following patterns are possible: LH, HH, and HL. LH is the most frequent noun pattern; the ratio of LH, HH, and HL nouns is an estimated 3:1:1. Trisyllabic nouns with the patterns LLH, LHL, HHH, and HLL are safely attested in our corpus. LLL is excluded; HLH does probably not exist. ... Baskeet distinguishes between H(H)-toned and L(L)-toned verbal stems. The combination of the stem with inflectional morphemes results in various tonal patterns.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (23 pp., text, the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Notes from the Field: Baskeet Phonological Sketch and Digital Wordlist', LD&C 8: 810-832). p. 9 = printed p. 818, §2.3.1 TONEMES: the quoted passage is there verbatim: 'Baskeet is a tonal language with two tonemes, high (H) and low (L). The syllable is the tone-bearing unit and tone occurs on each syllable. The importance of tone has so far been overlooked in the literature on Baskeet. Tone is, however, used to differentiate lexemes, and tonal minimal pairs are easily found, e.g. /zàrzàrá/ 'lizard' (Rec2-27) vs. /zàrzárà/ 'sieve' (Rec2-28)..'. The '[..]' bridges two sentences on tone-marking conventions; the final sentence reads in t…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Baskeet is a two-tone (H/L) language with tone on every syllable and lexical tonal contrasts; the authors explicitly reject an earlier one-high-tone-per-word (pitch accent) analysis. Word stress is never mentioned. §2.3.3 adds that all-low words do not occur in isolation (so every word carries at least one H: monosyllabic nouns are H; disyllabic nouns LH (most frequent, ~3:1:1), HH, HL; trisyllabic LLH, LHL, HHH, HLL; LLL excluded, HLH probably absent) and that verb stems are lexically H(H) or L(L). The older, superseded view (Inui 2005: 3, from speakers outside the area) was a lexically distinctive pitch accent whose position is not fixed, with few minimal pairs (buná 'coffee' vs búna 'flower').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (no stress described at all).
new_statements.exceptions: Ideophones can be all-low (fn 17); nouns become all-low when they drop the final high-toned vowel in compounds (fn 17); allotones (rising H, falling L) conditioned by position and preceding tone (§2.3.2); question intonation raises pitch on the penult with a fall on the lengthened final syllable (fn 44, p. 829).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone on citation forms recorded in isolation (2012 recordings, one main speaker cross-checked with others); tone rules in phrases and clauses not yet analysed (fn 31, p. 823).
new_statements.identity_note: Treis & Werth 2014 describe Baskeet as spoken inside the Basketo Special Woreda (main speaker Ambaye Tsedeke, cross-checked with other in-area speakers) = bask1236 proper; they state that Sottile 2002 and Inui 2005 analysed migrants' speech outside the area (Inui: three speakers in Bulki; earlier Arba Minch), which they say does not reflect the in-area variety. No separate dialect glottocode involved.

sources.note: §2.3 Tone (p. 818): Baskeet is a tonal language with two tonemes H and L, syllable is the TBU, tone on every syllable, lexical minimal pairs; explicitly rejects the pitch accent (one H per word) analyses of Sottile 2002 and Inui 2005. §2.3.3: no all-low words in isolation, disyllabic nouns LH (most frequent) / HH / HL, trisyllabic LLH, LHL, HHH, HLL. Nothing at all on stress; fn 44 (p. 829) describes question intonation (raised pitch on penult, fall on lengthened final).
